tellings.quote: The phenomenon reported is something real and not visionary or fictitious.

The reported operating characteristics such as extreme rates of climb, maneuverability (particularly in roll), and action which must be considered evasive when sighted or contacted by friendly aircraft and radar, lend belief to the possibility that some of the objects are controlled either manually, automatically or remotely.

It is possible within the present U. S. knowledge -- provided extensive detailed development is undertaken -- to construct a piloted aircraft which has the general description of the object in sub-paragraph (e) above which would be capable of an approximate range of 7000 miles at subsonic speeds.

Any developments in this country along the lines indicated would be extremely expensive, time consuming and at the considerable expense of current projects and therefore, if directed, should be set up independently of existing projects.
The possibility that these objects are of domestic origin - the product of some high security project not known to AC/AS-2 or this Command.

plain: In 1947 a top Air Force general wrote that flying discs were real, and, the host says, hinted that any effort to build such craft should be run as a separate program. The general was Nathan Twining, head of Air Materiel Command, the Army Air Forces command responsible for aircraft development, and his letter, known as the Twining memo, is dated 23 September 1947 and went to Brigadier General George Schulgen. Michels returns to it on many episodes, and its best known line is: "The phenomenon reported is something real and not visionary or fictitious." It also says the objects' "extreme rates of climb, maneuverability" and evasive action suggest some are "controlled either manually, automatically or remotely", and it raises the possibility that they come from "some high security project not known" to the Air Force's own intelligence or to Twining's command. What Michels calls a postscript is in the body of the letter: it says the US could "construct a piloted aircraft which has the general description of the object", and that any such work, if ordered, "should be set up independently of existing projects", which is the separate program he describes. The writer Marik von Rennenkampff tells it too, stressing Twining's later rise to chairman of the Joint Chiefs and the memo's list of UFO traits, and the television writer Bryce Zabel quotes the famous line. So the host and two guests all lean on the same official document. If read their way, the memo shows the military took the objects seriously from the start and pictured a separate secret effort around them.

discussion.by: AMC Opinion Concerning "Flying Discs" (the Twining memo)
discussion.text: The letter's own words (paragraph 2a) are "The phenomenon reported is something real and not visionary or fictitious", which the tellers give closely. What the host calls the memo's postscript is in the body of the letter: paragraph 2f says it is possible "to construct a piloted aircraft which has the general description of the object", and paragraph 2g that any such development, if directed, "should be set up independently of existing projects", the independent program the host describes.
